name: Botulinum toxin scalp mesotherapy

card.summary: Botulinum toxin A injected into the scalp, explored for hair thickness and scalp conditions such as androgenetic alopecia.
card.note: Off-label; evidence consists of small trials and case reports.

quick.overview:
Botulinum toxin scalp mesotherapy means injecting botulinum toxin type A into or around the scalp. People interested in hair density explore it because reduced scalp muscle tension and blood-flow changes are proposed to support hair growth.

Published work includes systematic reviews of botulinum toxin for scalp conditions and several small clinical trials in androgenetic alopecia; these report on trichoscopy and dermoscopy measures, and the research base remains early.
quick.how: A clinician injects the toxin into the scalp, either intradermally in thinning areas or into surrounding muscles; one split-scalp trial compared these two approaches. It is sometimes studied alongside other scalp treatments.
quick.risks: Off-label use for hair. Possible effects are those of botulinum toxin injections in general, such as local bruising or unwanted muscle weakness. Practitioners and researchers describe the evidence as still developing.

lead: Botulinum toxin scalp mesotherapy refers to injecting botulinum toxin type A into the scalp, an off-label approach investigated for androgenetic alopecia and other scalp conditions.[1]

People pursue it to thicken or retain hair for a fuller-looking hairline and crown. Proposed mechanisms include relaxation of scalp muscle tension and altered local blood flow, though these are hypotheses under study.[1]
A 2023 systematic review noted many reports of botulinum toxin for scalp conditions and sought to synthesise them; a 2020 systematic review covered 94 treated patients with alopecia.[1]

chain: Proposed reduction in scalp tension or change in local environment
angle.text: Proponents inject botulinum toxin into thinning areas hoping to improve hair density; the effect is under early investigation.

paras: The procedure delivers botulinum toxin A through multiple small scalp injections. A 2024 split-scalp randomised trial compared intradermal injection in the balding region with intramuscular injection in surrounding muscles.[1]

Controlled and comparative studies have tested botulinum toxin A in androgenetic alopecia: a 2022 comparative study contrasted it with scalp mesotherapy, a 2024 trial used ultrasound with trichoscopy, another assessed different toxin concentrations by dermoscopy, and a 2020 trial examined effectiveness and safety.[1] A 2024 paper described hair-to-hair trichoscopy as an objective outcome measure.[1] A 2026 case series combined botulinum toxin with PRP and stromal vascular fraction.[1] Overall conclusions are limited by small, heterogeneous studies.
A 2023 Dermatologic Surgery systematic review and a 2020 JPRAS systematic review synthesised reports on scalp use.[1]
